body:
Yes, let's fix this!

To be clear, is this from within an app directory or outside like the home directory?
This example was from the rails command as a standalone RubyGem in my user home directory, not within a created Rails app root directory.

One argument to your proposal could be that none of the commands actually work, or are relevant outside of a Rails application. I'm not sure it's useful showing a new user a long list of commands that don't do anything, or that would result in errors if run. The only one that does work outside a Rails app is the `new` command, which is why you get this help. Once inside a Rails application, the `rails --help` will display the full list of commands.

**tldr;** I think it's working as intended.

I can see it can be confusing to have the same command behave differently. 
Maybe we should have a ‘rails-new’ command instead?

I’ve also had this happen inside an app directory when I deleted the bin directory, trying to debug binstubs. Without bin/rails, Rails no longer thinks you are in an app directory and only allows ‘rails new’.

It would have been nice to have a ‘rails doctor’ command. Similar to ‘brew doctor’.

rename.to: No way to list common rails commands from CLI outside a rails app directory

body:
@aar0nr I take your point but regardless of usability, it should be possible to ask Rails to list its available commands rather than ignore input.

If the `rails` command is ignoring `--help` for any reason it should say so explicitely: 

Example:
```
cd ~
rails --help
$ rails --help
Only the `rails new` command works outside of a rails application directory.

You can use `rails new --help` for help on how to create new Rails application.

The most common rails commands are:
 generate     Generate new code (short-cut alias: "g")
 console      Start the Rails console (short-cut alias: "c")
 server       Start the Rails server (short-cut alias: "s")
 test         Run tests except system tests (short-cut alias: "t")
 test:system  Run system tests
 dbconsole    Start a console for the database specified in config/database.yml
              (short-cut alias: "db")

 new          Create a new Rails application. "rails new my_app" creates a
              new application called MyApp in "./my_app"

# ...
```

This is also a neat possible future tie in for any `rails new --interactive` options as mentioned in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/39444 and https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/t/interactive-rails-new/74355/22.

Essentially what I'm describing here is what could be in a `rails` manpage: 

```
$ man rails
No manual entry for rails
```

I don't think we want a new command but I agree with @olivierlacan that we should explicitly tell people that if they are not seeing the full list of commands is because they are either outside a Rails app or without the binstub.
@p8 do you want to work on that?
@p8 Down to pair on it if you’d like too by the way. Been diving in that code a bit.
@olivierlacan I'm currently off for the holidays, but I'll have time to work on this in january.

issue.title: Show default help when calling help outside a Rails application
issue.body:
### Summary

When running `rails -h` or just `rails` outside a Rails application,
Rails outputs all options for running the `rails new` command. This can be
confusing to users when they probably want to see the common Rails commands.

Instead, we should always show the common commands when running `rails -h`
inside or outside a Rails application.

With this change help works as follows...

Outside a Rails application we always show the default help when calling `rails`
without a command like `new`. 
We never show the extended commands: db:migrate, etc...
The extended commands require a Rails application.
They also take up a lot screen space.

- `rails`        outputs the help for the common commands
- `rails -h`     outputs the help for the common commands.
- `rails new -h` outputs the help for the new command.

Inside a Rails application it works mostly as before. The only change is
that calling plain `bin/rails` now only outputs the common commands and
not the extended commands.

- `bin/rails`    outputs the help for the common commands
- `bin/rails -h` outputs the help for the common commands and the
  extended commands

This is a work in progress for #40823 
cc @olivierlacan
